related_questions.question: How long do cats live after being diagnosed with diabetes?

text_blocks.snippet: Cats diagnosed with diabetes can live for varying lengths of time, with some living for years while others may have shorter lifespans. Many cats can live for several years with proper treatment and management of their diabetes, and some may even go into remission.

list.title: Median Survival:
list.snippet: Studies indicate the median survival time for diabetic cats is around 1.5 to 2 years after diagnosis.

list.title: Long-Term Survival:
list.snippet: However, some cats can live much longer, with some studies showing 25% of diabetic cats surviving for over 4 years. There are even cases of cats living 9 or 10 years after diagnosis.

list.title: Factors Affecting Lifespan:
list.snippet: Several factors influence how long a cat lives with diabetes, including:
Prompt and proper treatment: Early diagnosis and effective management with insulin, diet changes, and other therapies are crucial.
Complications: Concurrent diseases, like kidney problems or ketoacidosis, can negatively impact lifespan.
Remission: Some cats, particularly those diagnosed early and treated aggressively, can go into diabetic remission and no longer require insulin.
Quality of life: Maintaining a good quality of life for the cat is essential, and this depends on effective management of the diabetes and any related complications.

text_blocks.snippet: In summary, while there's no guarantee of a specific lifespan, with appropriate veterinary care and management, many cats with diabetes can live for a significant amount of time and enjoy a good quality of life.

related_questions.question: How much does cat diabetes cost to treat?

text_blocks.snippet: The cost to treat diabetes in cats varies widely, but can range from $50 to $250 or more per month. This includes costs for insulin, diabetic cat food, syringes, and regular vet visits. Some cats may require additional testing or medication, which can further increase the cost.

list.snippet: Insulin: Insulin costs can range from $30 to $100 per month.
Diabetic Cat Food: Expect to pay $25 to $80 per month, depending on the brand and whether you choose wet or dry food.
Syringes and Testing Supplies: Costs for these can range from $25 to $50 per month.
Veterinary Care: Regular checkups and monitoring can cost $100 to $200 per visit.

text_blocks.snippet: Additional factors that can affect costs:

list.title: Severity of Diabetes:
list.snippet: Cats with more severe cases may require more insulin and more frequent monitoring, increasing costs.

list.title: Home Monitoring:
list.snippet: If you choose to monitor your cat's blood glucose levels at home, you'll need to purchase a glucose monitor and test strips.

list.title: Remission:
list.snippet: Some cats can go into remission, potentially reducing or eliminating the need for insulin and other treatments, which can significantly lower long-term costs.

list.title: Location:
list.snippet: Vet costs can vary depending on your location.

text_blocks.snippet: Common signs of diabetes in cats include increased thirst and urination, increased appetite, and weight loss despite eating more. Cats may also exhibit lethargy, a dull coat, and a plantigrade stance (walking with their hocks on the ground). In severe cases, vomiting, dehydration, and a sweet-smelling breath can occur.
snippet_highlighted_words: increased thirst and urination, increased appetite, and weight loss despite eating more

list.title: Increased thirst and urination:
list.snippet: Cats with diabetes often drink more water than usual and urinate more frequently, sometimes flooding the litter box. This is because their kidneys are trying to flush out excess glucose from their system.

list.title: Increased appetite (polyphagia):
list.snippet: The body's cells are not getting enough glucose, so the brain signals that the cat is hungry, leading to increased food intake.

list.title: Weight loss:
list.snippet: Despite eating more, cats with diabetes may lose weight because their bodies are unable to utilize glucose properly and start breaking down fat and muscle for energy.

list.title: Lethargy and weakness:
list.snippet: Diabetic cats may become less active and show a general lack of energy.

list.title: Coat changes:
list.snippet: A dull, unkempt coat is another sign, as high blood sugar levels can affect skin and coat quality, leading to less frequent grooming.

list.title: Diabetic Neuropathy:
list.snippet: Nerve damage (neuropathy) can cause a change in gait, with some cats walking with their hocks on the ground or showing hind leg weakness.

list.title: Vomiting and diarrhea:
list.snippet: These can occur in some cases, especially with severe hyperglycemia or diabetic ketoacidosis.

list.title: Dehydration:
list.snippet: Increased urination can lead to dehydration, which can manifest as lethargy, tacky gums, or sunken eyes.

list.title: Sweet-smelling breath:
list.snippet: In advanced cases, a sweet, fruity odor on the breath can indicate diabetic ketoacidosis.
